Electronic Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China, 611731 (yhsu@uestc.edu.cn) 2. Institute for Wireless Intelligence, Chengdu, China Abstract- A shared-aperture antenna combining a sleeve monopole and a Vivaldi array is proposed for electromagnet spectrum map measurement. The operating frequency of 0.5–8 GHz is split into a low band (0.5–3.8 GHz) utilizing a vertically polarized sleeve monopole and a high band (3.8–8 GHz) utilizing a horizontally polarized Vivaldi array. Simulation results show a VSWR < 2.8 throughout the band, low-band gain variation < 1.5 dB, and stable high-band beam forming, suitable for spectrum monitoring scenarios. I. INTRODUCTION With the rapid advancement and widespread adoption of wireless communication technologies, electromagnetic spectrum resources are becoming increasingly scarce. The growing use of mobile communications, broadcasting, and emerging applications such as IoT and 5G/6G is driving a sharp increase in spectrum demand [1–3]. In this context, accurately characterizing the electromagnetic environment and effectively managing spectrum resources are crucial. Electromagnetic spectrum maps are typically produced by deploying fixed [4-5] or mobile [6] measurement nodes to collect power spectral density and band-occupancy data, which are then linked with geographic coordinates to create visualized representations that support spectrum planning, system optimization, and interference mitigation. Across a multi-octave frequency range from 0.5 GHz to 8 GHz, a single antenna often faces practical challenges such as large size, significant gain variation, or pattern distortion at higher frequencies [7-9]. Using multiple antennas to cover different bands can alleviate some of these issues, but it increases volume and installation complexity and may introduce mutual coupling [7-9]. Therefore, achieving ultra- wideband, omnidirectional coverage in a compact structure while reducing inter-band interference is key for efficient and accurate spectrum-map systems. Consequently, this work proposes a shared-aperture antenna, designed to meet the ultra-wideband coverage and omnidirectional radiation requirements of electromagnetic spectrum mapping applications. II. SHARED-APERTURE ANTENNA DESIGN A. Overall Structure The operational frequency band, 0.5 GHz–8 GHz, is divided into two non-overlapping sub-bands: (1) For 0.5 GHz–3.8 GHz, a sleeve monopole antenna serves as the low-frequency omnidirectional receiving unit, vertically polarized; (2) For 3.8 GHz–8 GHz, a Vivaldi antenna array with horizontal polarization is employed. Five Vivaldi radiating units are printed on a circular dielectric substrate. Each unit corresponds to approximately 72° of azimuth sector coverage. By exciting different units, distinct sectors can be covered, achieving equivalent 360° coverage. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the two sections are coaxially mounted. The low-frequency sleeve antenna occupies the central position, while the high-frequency Vivaldi antenna units are printed onto a circular dielectric substrate. This substrate features a central aperture and is mounted over the cylindrical sleeve of the low-frequency antenna, thereby forming a shared-aperture structure. Due to the non- overlapping frequency bands and differing polarization modes of the two sub-bands, the mutual coupling between structures is minimized. B. Sleeve Monopole Antenna The low-frequency band spans 0.5 GHz to 3.8 GHz, employing a sleeve monopole antenna. This design builds upon the monopole antenna by adding a coaxially mounted metal sleeve, effectively broadening the monopole antenna's operational bandwidth. Modifying the geometric shape and physical dimensions of the radiator and sleeve can expand the antenna's impedance bandwidth. The structure and dimension of the antenna is presented in Fig. 2, comprising four components: the central radiator, the sleeve, the loading metal ring, and the ground plane. The central radiator consists of a solid cylindrical section connected to the coaxial cable's inner conductor, topped by a hollow conical frustum with a wall thickness of 0.8 mm. The loading metal ring is nested onto the solid cylindrical section of the Figure 1. Overall structure of the entire antenna. central radiator. The sleeve is positioned on the ground plane with a wall thickness of 1.5 mm. This antenna achieves both vertical polarization and near- omnidirectional radiation pattern. Concurrently, the hollow conical frustum of the central radiator, combined with the sleeve configuration and capacitive ring, facilitates impedance bandwidth expansion and enhances pattern stability. C. Annular Vivaldi Antenna Array The high-frequency band spans 3.8 GHz to 8 GHz, employing the directional radiation mechanism of Vivaldi antennas. This achieves multi-sector coverage across a 360° azimuth by arranging elements in a circular, equiangular pattern. The structure and dimension of the antenna is presented in Fig. 3, comprising three principal components: The Vivaldi metallic radiating elements, the feed structure, and the circular dielectric substrate. Five Vivaldi radiators are uniformly distributed on the annular dielectric substrate, with adjacent units spaced at 72° intervals. Each Vivaldi unit comprises a metallized gradient slot line, and features three slits along its edge, including one longitudinal slit and two transverse slits, designed to broaden the unit's radiation beam width. Each Vivaldi radiating unit connects to a feed point via a 50Ω microstrip line. A substrate with a dielectric constant of 2.1 and thickness of 1 mm is adopted. It features a central aperture designed to mount externally on the sleeve structure of the sleeve antenna. Furthermore, the Vivaldi radiating elements and feed structures are printed on the upper and lower surfaces of the dielectric substrate respectively. As this annular array of Vivaldi antennas is horizontally polarized and operates in a frequency band non-overlapping with the low-frequency range, mutual coupling between the two antennas is mitigated. III. SIMULATION RESULT To validate the performance of the designed antennas, a full- wave simulation analysis was conducted. Fig. 4 presents the VSWR simulation results for the sleeve antenna and the Vivaldi antennas. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), the sleeve antenna achieves VSWR < 2.8 across the entire 0.5 GHz to 3.8 GHz frequency band, realizing a bandwidth ratio as high as 7.6:1. Fig. 4 (b) indicates that the Vivaldi radiating unit maintains VSWR < 2.8 across its 3.8 GHz to 8 GHz operating band, corresponding to a bandwidth ratio of 2.1. The combined operation of both antenna sections effectively achieves continuous broadband coverage. Fig. 5 to Fig. 8 present the radiation pattern simulation results. For the low-frequency band sleeve antenna, the E-plane radiation pattern in Fig. 5 indicates the gain variation of its main-beam polarization is less than 1.5 dB across the operating band, demonstrating excellent omnidirectionality. Combined with the H-plane pattern in Fig. 6, it shows that the cross- polarization levels within both E-plane and H-plane are Figure 2. Structure of the sleeve monopole antenna (unit: mm). Figure 3. For the high-frequency Vivaldi antenna, Fig. 7 (a) displays the E-plane radiation characteristics of the unit, achieving a 3 dB beamwidth of approximately 72° across the entire operating band. The H-plane radiation characteristics shown in Fig. 7 (b) indicate that the main radiation direction consistently maintains 𝜃𝜃 =90° throughout the frequency range. Subsequently, Fig. 8 further presents the effect of combining the azimuth beams from all high-frequency Vivaldi elements. The results demonstrate that this configuration achieves equivalent 360° omnidirectional radiation coverage across the operating frequency band. IV. CONCLUSION This paper designs and validates an ultra-wideband shared- aperture antenna covering 0.5–8 GHz. By employing a vertically polarized sleeve monopole with a horizontally polarized Vivaldi array, the antenna achieves continuous ultra- wideband coverage, effectively resolving the radiation pattern distortion issue at high frequency inherent in single ultra- wideband antennas. Simultaneously, the polarization orthogonality reduces mutual coupling between heterogeneous elements. Simulation results demonstrate excellent impedance matching (VSWR < 2.8) and stable omnidirectional radiation performance, establishing this antenna as an efficient solution for electromagnetic spectrum monitoring.
